title: The Rice Cooker That Failed on the Third Floor of Shirokiya
dek: In late 1945 Masaru Ibuka's new workshop in a damaged Tokyo department store built an electric rice cooker that would not cook rice, and went back to fixing radios.

story.event: Abandoning a failed electric rice cooker in a rented department-store room and returning to radio work before founding the company
story.summary: In October 1945 Masaru Ibuka and a few former colleagues set up Tokyo Tsushin Kenkyujo in a rented room on the third floor of the Shirokiya department store in Nihonbashi, Tokyo, repairing and modifying radios. Their electric rice cooker, a wooden tub with aluminium electrodes, mostly undercooked or overcooked the rice and was abandoned. With Akio Morita, Ibuka founded Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo on 7 May 1946 with 190,000 yen of capital; it took the name Sony in 1958.
paragraphs: In the autumn of 1945, Masaru Ibuka, an engineer of 37, brought a handful of colleagues from their wartime evacuation site in Suzaka, Nagano, to a rented room of about thirty square metres on the third floor of the Shirokiya department store in Nihonbashi, Tokyo. Even the window glass was missing. In October they hung a plaque naming themselves Tokyo Tsushin Kenkyujo, the Tokyo Telecommunications Research Institute.

Ibuka's reasoning, as Sony's official history records it, was that the giant pre-war firms would come back and a small group could not beat them head-on, so he looked for work they would not bother with. People wanted news from the outside world, and the team repaired radios and modified them to pick up shortwave broadcasts, a trade that grew after the Asahi Shimbun wrote about it.

He also wanted to make something for daily life. Electricity was more plentiful than fuel, and Ibuka bought a truckload of wooden tubs to turn into electric rice cookers, with aluminium electrodes fixed to the bottom. They worked only when the rice was of consistent quality, he said, and much of what could be had was not. Most batches came out undercooked or overcooked. "I remember sitting there on the third floor in Shirokiya day after day being fed rice that wasn't fit to eat," he later recalled. Sony's history calls the cooker his "Failed Prototype No. 1".

He dropped it. The team went back to radios and to a vacuum-tube voltmeter that government offices had begun to order, and by the end of 1945 the business was finding its feet. A later stopgap, an electrically heated cushion of fine wire glued between sheets of paper, sold because there was little else to buy, but it scorched futons, and Ibuka lost sleep fearing a fire.

Akio Morita, a young navy lieutenant Ibuka had met during the war, read about the radios and wrote to him. On 7 May 1946 they founded Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo with 190,000 yen of capital and, by Sony's count, just over twenty people. "We're no match for the industry giants if we do the same things as them," Ibuka said at the founding. In 1958 the company took the name Sony.

quote.text: he discerns the limits of his powers, and by doing what he knows, he provides himself with what he needs and so does well; or, conversely, by holding aloof from what he knows not, he avoids mistakes and thereby mishaps.
quote.locator: Book IV, Chapter II (Socrates to Euthydemus on "Know thyself")
quote.source_title: The Memorabilia, tr. Henry Graham Dakyns, Project Gutenberg eBook #1177
quote.connection: Xenophon's Socrates praises the person who knows where their powers end and keeps to what they know. That fits Ibuka's retreat from rice cookers to radios. It fits less well a founder whose stated plan was to do what the big companies could not, which meant working beyond what anyone yet knew.

reflection: Ibuka did not hide the rice cooker. He gave it a number, which quietly assumes there will be others, and went back to the radio work people would pay for while he worked out what came next. Neither move looks heroic. Both kept the work going.

You may have something of your own that is half working, and something steadier that pays for the time. Socrates would call keeping to the steady thing good sense; Ibuka's later work says that is not the whole answer. For today it can be both: the first set aside without being called finished, and the second done without apology.
invitation: Pick one thing you tried that did not work and give it a plain label and a number, the way Ibuka did. Write one line on what it taught you, then leave it there for today.

sources.supports: Ibuka's meeting with navy lieutenant Akio Morita during the war; the move from Suzaka, Nagano, with colleagues from Nihon Sokuteiki to a thirty-odd square metre room on the third floor of Shirokiya in Nihonbashi, missing its window glass; the Tokyo Tsushin Kenkyujo plaque in October 1945; Ibuka's reasoning about the returning industrial giants; radio modifications and repairs for shortwave reception and the Asahi Shimbun Blue Pencil column; Morita writing to Ibuka after seeing the article; the rice cooker (wooden pot with aluminium electrodes) that would not cook evenly, called 'Failed Prototype No. 1'; vacuum-tube voltmeters ordered by government offices and the company on track by the end of 1945; the 1946 heated cushion of nichrome wire between paper that scorched futons and cost Ibuka sleep; founding on 7 May 1946 with 190,000 yen and just over twenty people; Ibuka's founding remark.

sources.title: The Battle to Invent the Automatic Rice Cooker (Anne Ewbank, 31 July 2020), archived copy
sources.publisher: Atlas Obscura (Gastro Obscura), via the Internet Archive
sources.supports: Ibuka's 1945 workshop in a vacant department store; electricity relatively plentiful while fuel was expensive; Ibuka buying a truckload of wooden tubs; the cookers working only with rice of consistent quality, by Ibuka's account; Ibuka's recollection of being fed rice 'that wasn't fit to eat' on the third floor of Shirokiya (quoted from John Nathan's Sony: The Private Life); return to fixing radios; the company becoming known as Sony in 1958.

cross_checks.claim: In autumn 1945 Ibuka set up his workshop, Tokyo Tsushin Kenkyujo, in a damaged building (the Shirokiya department store) in Tokyo, repairing radios.
The electric rice cooker, a wooden tub with electrodes at the bottom, mostly undercooked or overcooked the rice and was abandoned.
The heated cushion scorched bedding and Ibuka feared it would cause a fire.
Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo was founded in May 1946 with capital of 190,000 yen, and Ibuka spoke at the founding about not competing as the big companies did.
The company took the name Sony in 1958.

research_notes: Year: the slate gave 1946; Sony's own history dates the rice cooker to Tokyo Tsushin Kenkyujo in 1945 (photo caption 'Electric Rice Cooker (Tokyo Tsushin Kenkyujo, 1945)') and the plaque to October 1945, with incorporation as Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo on 7 May 1946, so approx_date is 1945-10. Staff numbers disagree: Sony's history gives 'just over twenty people' at the May 1946 founding; The Independent's 1997 obituary says the company 'employed 36 people'; Commoncog's summary of John Nathan's book (not cited) says seven employees followed Ibuka at the very start. The story uses Sony's figure and attributes it ('by Sony's count'). Ibuka's founding remark exists in two translations: Sony's ('We're no match for the industry giants if we do the same things as them') and The Independent's ('We can never achieve anything if we try to do things as big companies do'); the story quotes Sony's wording. Gizmodo credits the rice cooker to 'Ibuka and Morita', but Sony's history shows Morita joined only in 1946, after the cooker; the story treats it as Ibuka's project. Ibuka's recollection about rice 'that wasn't fit to eat' is quoted by Atlas Obscura from John Nathan's Sony: The Private Life (1999), p. 13; the truckload of tubs and the dependence on rice quality also come from Atlas Obscura's retelling. The heated cushion followed in 1946 (Sony) and is described as a later stopgap. Atlas Obscura blocks automated requests, so its article is cited from the Internet Archive copy of 5 December 2023. The sony.com page loaded for the source checker at first and later returned 403 under repeated requests. Funding: Totsuken ran on its own earnings in 1945; for the 1946 company Sony's history says Ibuka's father-in-law Tamon Maeda became president to help with capital and that Michiji Tajima and Teikoku Bank chairman Junshiro Mandai backed the funding. The episode itself (late 1945) was self-funded, so 'bootstrapped' is kept. Quote: Socrates' advice to Euthydemus in Memorabilia IV.ii (conventionally around section 26); applied by analogy.
